query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings, a refined (fine‐grained) microstructure promotes the rapid formation and enhanced stability of a continuous, protective oxide/glaze layer that reduces friction and wear. This stable interfacial layer accommodates plastic deformation and prevents direct adhesive and abrasive interactions, thereby governing superior wear performance compared to coatings with a coarse microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy protective coating (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi or a similar system) that in its as‐fabricated state exhibits a mixed microstructure with both fine and coarse grains.
generation.intervention: Processing modification (e.g., annealing, friction stir processing, or controlled cooling) to obtain a refined, fine-grained microstructure in the coating.
generation.conditions: Wear tests performed under sliding conditions (typical contact loads and moderate-to-high sliding speeds) in an oxidizing environment where glaze/oxide formation is feasible.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuous, stable oxide (glaze) layer formed at the friction interface, whose integrity is mediated by the underlying fine-grain microstructure and high surface hardness.
generation.mechanism: Fine grains increase the surface hardness and enhance uniform deformation during sliding, which facilitates the early formation of a coherent oxide layer that resists cracking and delamination. This protective layer prevents direct metal-to-metal contact and reduces both adhesive and abrasive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings with a refined microstructure will exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates due to the formation of a stable protective oxide layer, whereas coatings with a coarse grain structure will show more oxide layer rupture, higher plastic deformation, and increased wear.
generation.baseline: Coatings with a predominantly coarse-grained microstructure that form less continuous or more brittle oxide layers under similar wear conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold over a range of typical wear loads and sliding speeds in oxidizing environments; its applicability might be limited in inert atmospheres or under conditions where alternative wear mechanisms (e.g., severe plastic deformation unrelated to oxide stability) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise correlation between grain size refinement and oxide layer stability may vary with alloy composition, processing parameters, and environmental conditions. It is also not clear how extreme loads or temperatures might shift the balance between beneficial oxide protection and detrimental softening.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy coatings that differ only in their grain size (one set processed to exhibit a fine-grained microstructure and the other a coarse-grained microstructure). Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under controlled load, speed, and environmental (oxidizing) conditions. Use surface characterization (e.g., SEM coupled with EDS) to assess oxide/glaze layer continuity and integrity and measure friction coefficients and wear rates.
measurements: Grain size distribution via electron microscopy
Specific wear rate (e.g., mass loss or volume loss per N·m)
Continuity and thickness of the oxide/glaze layer via SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained coatings do not form a more continuous and stable oxide layer and do not exhibit significantly lower friction coefficients and wear rates relative to the coarse-grained coatings, then the hypothesis that grain refinement governs wear resistance via enhanced protective oxide layer formation is falsified.

This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.

AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism

In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.
